articles_hidden.title: Cortex-wide imaging in naturally behaving mice with 1-gram wireless mesoscopes
articles_hidden.authors: Yuanlong Zhang, Angran Li, Lekang Yuan, Mingrui Wang, Weihao Zhao, Zhenbo Wang, Boyang Zang, Yangxuan Zhou, Tao Yu, Lin Gao, Yu Wu, Rongkang Zhu, Mengyi Tian, Kun Li, Jiamin Wu, Pu Dai, Qionghai Dai
articles_hidden.abstract: Revealing how distributed cortical circuits coordinate behavior in freely moving animals remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience, constrained by limited fields of view, low throughput, and the tethering required by current miniaturized microscopes1-4. Here, we present Airscope, a wireless mesoscope delivering 4 μm lateral resolution across a 6 mm field of view at 12.5 Hz, weighing 1.0 gram. An aspheric-lens design achieves a 2.84× shorter total track length than previous miniaturized microscopes1,2,5,6 while matching the neuron yield of benchtop one-photon mesoscopes; a tailored wireless link supports cable-free calcium imaging from >8,500 neurons per animal (25‑fold increase). Paired with a zero-shot behavior analyzer, Airscope enables cortical imaging across rich behavioral conditions, including room-scale enriched arenas, swimming assays, and multi-organ implantation, with concurrent recording from multiple animals. Using Airscope, we demonstrate versatile applications of untethered cortical imaging across diverse behavioral paradigms. We identify cortical activity patterns across multiple dorsal regions that correlate with behavioral signatures of social dominance, and show dorsal-cortical population activity prospectively decodes competition outcomes across paired animals. We observe reward-location-associated cortical activity patterns during maze exploration, and characterize Granger-causal influence from spinal cord to cortex during fear conditioning, enabled by simultaneous brain-spinal recordings. By uniting large-scale, cellular-resolution recording with unconstrained behavior, Airscope makes naturalistic, multi-animal cortical recording experimentally practical, and provides a broadly accessible technology for systems neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control
articles_hidden.authors: Fan Yu, Lingyu Jiang, Hanyu Liu, Song Yang, Yuan Yuan, Hongzhen Jin, Jinming Liu, Xi Liu, Yu Dong, Dongfeng Ren, Jie Kang, Yan Huang, Qi Meng, Feng Bai, Yanjun Li, Shuoguo Li, Huadong Liu, Wei Zhao, Jia Xiao, Quan Chen
articles_hidden.abstract: Mitochondria are bound by a double membrane and are semiautonomous organelles, rendering them highly vulnerable to global and internal proteostatic stress1. Multiple surveillance mechanisms at proteostatic and inter-organellar levels have evolved to maintain mitochondrial integrity and cellular health2,3,4,5,6,7. However, the precise mechanisms by which proteostatic damage relays stress signals across organelles and how the quality surveillance machinery coordinates these functions remain unknown. Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network. Quantitative proteomic and correlative light–electron microscopy analysis revealed that SIMPA mediates inter-organellar communication via mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes. Mechanistically, GRP75 coordinates SIMPA biogenesis and focally activates endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response pathways via mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes for the targeted clearance of SIMPAs. Functionally, in both cellular and liver disease models, we found that a GRP75-dependent SIMPA signalling cascade attenuates mitochondrial stress and preserves mitochondrial integrity under proteotoxic stress. Overall, we show that SIMPAs, functioning as protein condensates, serve as a central cross-compartment communication hub for mitochondrial quality control, supporting cellular and organismal fitness.

articles_hidden.title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes
articles_hidden.authors: Kwang-Soo Kim, Cory Gardner, Alissa Cullen, Jalin A. Stelzer, Kevin Cho, Ashish Sharma, Mati T. Nemera, Travis Law, Huma Naz, Guoyan Zhao, Harrison W. Gabel, Gary J. Patti, Erik S. Musiek, Tae-Hyuk Ahn, Jason J. Yi
articles_hidden.abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.

articles_hidden.authors: A. Ali Heydari, Ken Gu, Vidya Srinivas, Hong Yu, Akshay Paruchuri, Zhihan Zhang, Yuwei Zhang, Qian He, Hamid Palangi, Nova Hammerquist, Ahmed A. Metwally, Brent Winslow, Yubin Kim, Kumar Ayush, Yuzhe Yang, Girish Narayanswamy, Maxwell A. Xu, Jake Garrison, Samuel Schmidgall, Amy Armento Lee, Jenny Vafeiadou, Ben Graef, Isaac R. Prieto, Conor Heneghan, Jiening Zhan, Mark Malhotra, Shwetak Patel, Yun Liu, Tim Althoff, Xin Liu, Daniel McDuff, Xuhai Orson Xu
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored 1,2 . Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: WEE1 opposes APC/CCDH1 activity to promote S phase entry
articles_hidden.authors: Luc-Alban Vuillemenot, Lucas G. Morales, Calin-Mihai Dragoi, Betheney R. Pennycook, Edward Harris, Liuyang C. Lin, William A. Weston, Jade-Ellen Brown, Emma Graham, Leelou Moulin, Ivan Andrew, Georgia Roumelioti, Alex Montoya, Laurence Game, George R. Young, Keshava K. Datta, Pavel Shliaha, Béla Novák, Hiroyuki Yamano, Alexis R. Barr
articles_hidden.abstract: WEE1 phosphorylates and inhibits the activity of cyclin-dependent kinases to prevent mitotic entry and establish a G2 DNA damage checkpoint 1–3 . Consequently, WEE1 inhibitors have been developed to be synthetically lethal in TP53- mutated tumours that become reliant on this WEE1-mediated checkpoint, and such inhibitors are undergoing clinical trials. However, WEE1 inhibitors also have efficacy in TP53- wild-type tumours, and many trials have been terminated owing to high levels of toxic side effects, suggesting that WEE1 has unknown functions. Here we show that WEE1 promotes cell cycle re-entry from quiescence (G0) by opposing the activity of the E3 ubiquitin ligase, anaphase-promoting complex–cyclosome bound to CDH1 (APC/C CDH1 ). WEE1 phosphorylates CDH1 ( FZR1 ) at key residues that mediate the interaction between CDH1 and APC/C. Cells with loss of function of WEE1 during G0/G1 have delayed S phase entry, impaired G1/S transition, abnormal S phase accumulation of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21 Cip1/Kip1 and a p21-dependent G2 arrest. Reduced expression of APC/C CDH1 or p21 renders cells more sensitive to acute WEE1 inhibition, and both pathways are downregulated in cells with acquired WEE1 inhibitor resistance. These results reveal a mechanism of cell cycle control that has implications for how WEE1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.

articles_hidden.title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement
articles_hidden.authors: Liang Qi, Yingying Sheng, Wenna Zhang, Youming Ni, Linhai He, Bin Li, Anjie Wang, Wenliang Zhu, Alexis T. Bell, Zhongmin Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1,2,3,4,5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6,7,8,9,10,11,12. Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13. Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14,15,16,17,18. Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation. We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h. The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively. Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation. Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes.

articles_hidden.title: The proteome of Middle Pleistocene Xujiayao and common Denisovan morphology
articles_hidden.authors: Song Xing, Zhongyou Wu, Qingfeng Shao, Junyi Ge, E. Andrew Bennett, Huiyun Rao, Sungui Lin, Yuhao Zhao, Feng Liu, Yichen Liu, Kai Zhou, Xiaotian Feng, Qigao Jiangzuo, Qiaomei Fu
articles_hidden.abstract: The taxonomy and phylogeny of late Middle Pleistocene hominins in East Asia remain highly debated1. Xujiayao, a key representative assemblage with many fossils and a clear stratigraphy dating to around 199–138 thousand years ago, has been extensively studied, but its evolutionary position remains uncertain. Here, to clarify this, we analysed Xujiayao material through both palaeoproteomic analysis and morphological comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo. Proteomic analysis of two specimens identified 18 endogenous proteins, and the Denisova-specific COL1A2-996 R>K mutation strongly supported their affiliation with the Denisovan lineage. Extended analysis identifies a set of shared morphological traits between Denisovan fossils (Xujiayao and Harbin) and other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo (such as Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong), indicating that they all belong to the Denisovan lineage. This analysis provides a comprehensive view of Denisovan features, showing both traits reminiscent of Homo erectus (such as a thick cranial vault) and those characteristic of modern humans (for example, a strongly arched temporal squama). They also share features with late Neanderthals, such as the structure of the temporal labyrinth and the presence of a suprainiac fossa. Notably, Denisovans are distinctive, with a low cranial profile with near-parallel lateral walls, a massive supraorbital torus, a flat zygomaxillary region and weak prognathism.

articles_hidden.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
articles_hidden.authors: Hyun Ju Lee, Cansu Doğan, Seda Koyuncu, Markus Wehrmann, Murat Artan, Dunja Petrovic, Rute Loureiro, Amit Kumar Sahu, Joana Schnubel, Pavel Grobushkin, Dimitrios Prymidis, Theodoros Georgomanolis, Agnieszka Sokol, Ming Yang, Thorsten Hoppe, Christian Frezza, David Vilchez
articles_hidden.abstract: Moderately cold temperatures extend lifespan and promote health across species 1–3 , yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these benefits remain unclear. Here we define a metabolite-driven, multi-tissue signalling system that links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans . Cold temperature upregulates the biopterin-synthesis enzyme CAT-4 (GCH1 in humans), increasing production of dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a transportable reservoir for the bioactive cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH2 is produced in muscle and transported to distal tissues, including the intestine and neurons, where it is converted into BH4 by the salvage enzyme DHFR-1. BH4 functions as an essential cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase PAH-1, promoting tyrosine synthesis and extending lifespan. This BH2–BH4 axis also prevents disease-related protein aggregation and subsequent neuronal dysfunction during ageing. Importantly, increasing BH2 synthesis specifically in muscle is sufficient to promote longevity and suppress pathological protein aggregation in distal tissues, even at normal or elevated temperatures. In human cells, BH2 or tyrosine supplementation reduces aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins associated with Huntington’s disease, as well as mutant variants of TDP-43 and FUS that cause amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Together, these findings identify BH2 as a cold-induced metabolite of which the synthesis, intertissue transport and conversion into bioactive BH4 preserve organism-wide proteostasis and extend lifespan.

articles_hidden.title: Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance
articles_hidden.authors: Anil Kumar Singh, León Martin, Matea Sršen, Freja Schou Guttesen, Bing-Zhong Hu, Yuta Ito, Stephan Korsgaard Pedersen, Fadhil Suleiman Kamounah, Fabian Pauly, Michael Pittelkow, Jing-Tao Lü, Per Hedegård, Oren Tal
articles_hidden.abstract: For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage’s polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4–6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.

articles_hidden.title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis
articles_hidden.authors: Yue Yi, Zuorong Cao, Kejia Wu, Hengwu Ding, Lin Fu, Wenyi Gao, Ling Li, Lei Zhou, Zhuo Zhou, Lirong Dai, Yahai Lu, Lei Cheng
articles_hidden.abstract: Anaerobic degradation of complex organic compounds to methane and carbon dioxide is common in the deep subsurface biosphere and has long been considered to require syntrophic cooperation, with methanogens confined to the terminal use of simple C1 and C2 substrates. Thermodynamic considerations, multi-omics analyses and microcosm experiments suggest that archaeal lineages are capable of methanogenic degradation of complex substrates1,2,3,4,5,6. However, experimental validation in pure culture was lacking. Here we report the isolation of a thermophilic archaeon, Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75, affiliated with Archaeoglobi, from a Chinese petroleum reservoir. Strain AA-75 not only converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, but also uses saturated fatty acids varying from C7:0 to C18:0 and unsaturated fatty acids including C16:1, C18:1 and C18:2 to produce methane. We term the latter lipotrophic methanogenesis, which integrates β-oxidation of fatty acids with the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway and the canonical methyl-tetrahydromethanopterin:coenzyme M methyltransferase and methyl-coenzyme M reductase complexes, together with an intracellular electron transfer system. A formaldehyde-methanol branch probably functions as an auxiliary route for C1 metabolism during methanogenesis. Methane produced from stearate is moderately 13C-enriched (δ13C–CH4 = −40.0‰ to −36.3‰), distinct from the strong 13C depletion characteristic of canonical methanogenic pathways. These findings demonstrate that methanogens can function as primary degraders of complex organic matter, challenging the classical syntrophic paradigm and calling for refinement of current models of carbon cycling in the deep subsurface biosphere.

articles_hidden.title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root
articles_hidden.authors: Marina Oliva, Tim Stuart, Dave Tang, Adil Khan, Olivier Clement, Dawid Makosa, Daniel Poppe, Jahnvi Pflueger, Jafar S. Jabbari, Scott Gigante, Jonathan Michael Dragwidge, Milly Petterson, James Whelan, Mathew G. Lewsey, Ryan Lister
articles_hidden.abstract: Plant development is highly plastic, with growth and architecture continuously shaped by environmental conditions. Roots, for instance, adjust their development to local water, nutrient and soil conditions. Despite this plasticity, individual root cell types are generally viewed as largely homogeneous populations that progress along a single developmental trajectory1. Here we show that rather than progressing along a single developmental trajectory, most Arabidopsis root cell lineage trajectories exhibit a stereotyped bifid topology, as revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcript mapping. One branch is characterized by a transcriptional program that is shared across multiple cell types and enriched for genes associated with environmental responses, including abscisic acid (ABA) signalling. This state occurs reproducibly in a subset of cells across multiple cell types, independent of developmental lineage, thereby revealing an additional layer of root cell identity. It is conserved across Arabidopsis ecotypes and persists despite major perturbations in developmental identity. Moreover, it is reduced in ABA-deficient and ABA-insensitive mutants and becomes more prevalent under water-deficit conditions. Together, these findings reveal an additional layer of root cell identity that is superimposed on developmental lineage and its prevalence is modulated by environmental conditions. These results uncover a previously unrecognized source of environment-associated transcriptional heterogeneity shared across root cell types.

articles_hidden.title: Octupole-driven spin torque switching of antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions
articles_hidden.authors: Jaimin Kang, Mohammad Hamdi, Shun Kong Cheung, Lin-Ding Yuan, Mohamed Elekhtiar, Eric Matt, William Rogers, Andrea Meo, Peter G. Lim, M. S. Nicholas Tey, Anthony D’Addario, Shiva T. Konakanchi, Jordan Athas, Sevdenur Arpaci, Antoine Devincenti, Lei Wan, Sanjay C. Mehta, Nicholas Zogbi, Vinod K. Sangwan, Jean Anne C. Incorvia, Jennifer Fowlie, Pramey Upadhyaya, Mario Carpentieri, Vinayak P. Dravid, Mark C. Hersam, Jordan A. Katine, Gregory D. Fuchs, Giovanni Finocchio, Evgeny Y. Tsymbal, James M. Rondinelli, Pedram Khalili Amiri
articles_hidden.abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions based on ferromagnets are canonical devices in spintronics, with wide-ranging applications in data storage, computing and sensing. They simultaneously exhibit mechanisms for electrical detection and control of magnetic order through the tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR)1,2,3,4,5 and spin-transfer torque6,7,8,9 effects, respectively. It was long assumed that neither of these effects could be sizeable in all-antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions (AATJs), considering that they have no net magnetization. However, it was recently shown that AATJs based on chiral antiferromagnets do exhibit TMR due to their non-relativistic momentum-dependent spin polarization and cluster magnetic octupole moment, which are manifestations of their spin–split band structure10,11,12,13. However, the reciprocal effect, that is, the antiferromagnetic counterpart of spin–transfer torque, has been assumed non-existent due to the total electric current being spin-neutral. Here we report nanoscale AATJs that display this reciprocal effect, which we term octupole-driven spin-transfer torque (OTT). We demonstrate current-induced OTT switching of PtMn3|MgO|PtMn3 AATJs, with a TMR value of 363% at room temperature and switching current densities of the order of 10 MA cm–2. Our theoretical modelling explains the origin of OTT in terms of the imbalance between intra- and inter-sublattice spin currents across the AATJ, and, equivalently, in terms of the non-zero net cluster octupole polarization of each PtMn3 layer. This work establishes a new materials platform for antiferromagnetic spintronics and provides a pathway towards deeply scaled magnetic memory and room-temperature terahertz technologies.

articles_hidden.title: Additive manufacturing of ultralong and architected single crystals
articles_hidden.authors: Changmeng Liu, Yinan Cui, Jiachen Wang, Xiao Han, Zhongao Ji, Zhun Liang, Chongle Zhang, Jaime Marian, Zixiang Li, Tao Lu, Tianqiu Xu, Jinyu Zhang, Wei Cui, Wei Liu, Daining Fang, Y. Morris Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Single-crystal materials are indispensable for high-performance applications, yet their deployment remains constrained by conventional manufacturing techniques that depend on strict quasi-steady thermal conditions1. This requirement fundamentally conflicts with the intense cyclic thermal fluctuations inherent to additive manufacturing2, historically preventing the 3D printing of large or architected single crystals. Here we present a free-form additive manufacturing approach that resolves this contradiction by using delicately controlled alternating and pulsed heat inputs to govern and direct single-crystal growth. Using this method, we demonstrate the fabrication of metre-tall, centimetre-diameter single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V alongside, to our knowledge, the first single-crystal lattice structures containing complex zigzag ligaments, effectively eliminating theoretical size constraints for single-crystal components. The resulting bulk single-crystal Ti-6Al-4V exhibits an order-of-magnitude increase in creep resistance over standard grain-size scaling predictions, driven by the synergistic elimination of grain boundaries and an additive manufacturing-induced hierarchical α/β-architecture that regulates dislocation density, mobility and void evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broad applicability of this technique by printing single crystals of hard-to-process refractory metals, including W, Mo, Nb and MoNb alloys. Our work introduces a large-scale method for single-crystal additive manufacturing, expanding the accessible materials library and enabling high-performance, complex geometries previously unattainable by classical methods.

articles_hidden.title: Enzyme-embedded polyesters for accelerated biodegradation in the deep sea
articles_hidden.authors: QiuYuan Huang, Noriko Iida, Noriyuki Isobe, Taizo Kabe, Taku Omura, Manikandan Ilangovan, Satoshi Kimura, Jin Ho Seok, Hidetaka Nomaki, Ken-ichi Kasuya, Tadahisa Iwata
articles_hidden.abstract: The accumulation of persistent plastics in the ocean is causing wide-ranging environmental problems 1–3 . Some commercially available compostable plastics 4–7 , developed to address these issues, degrade efficiently under industrial composting conditions; however, their degradation in marine environments, particularly in the deep sea, remains limited 8–10 . Here we demonstrate that thermally embedding enzymes into compostable polyesters (poly(butylene succinate) (PBS), poly(butylene succinate- co -adipate) (PBSA), poly(ε-caprolactone) (PCL) and poly(butylene adipate- co -terephthalate) (PBAT)) significantly accelerates their degradation in both coastal and deep-sea environments from water depths of 2–6 m to 5,503 m. Enzyme-embedded polyesters achieved near-complete degradation at a deep-sea depth of 757 m within 5 months. Furthermore, moderate biodegradation of enzyme-embedded polyesters was observed under extreme conditions on deep-sea floors of 5,503 m. In coastal seawater, films embedded with trace amounts (0.1 wt%) of enzyme underwent rapid degradation. The mechanical properties of enzyme-embedded polyesters were similar to those of enzyme-free polyesters. Chemical analysis confirmed the formation of low-molecular-mass degradation products and biochemical oxygen demand measurements supported the mineralization of the enzyme-embedded polyesters. The enzyme-embedding strategy enables enhanced marine degradation of compostable polyesters and represents a potential solution to marine plastic pollution.

articles_hidden.title: Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses
articles_hidden.authors: Leandro Battini, Megan M. Slough, Ramandeep Kaur, Luqiang Guo, Catalina Florez, Alexandra Serris, Annalisa Meola, Gorka Lasso, Nicole D. Tischler, Raymond Alvarez, Upendra P. Lambe, Lohit Khera, Jian Wang, Rona S. Scott, Jose L. Garrido, Maria I. Barria, Nicole M. Josleyn, Félix A. Rey, Andrew S. Herbert, Jason S. McLellan, Rohit K. Jangra, Kartik Chandran, Pablo Guardado-Calvo
articles_hidden.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.

articles_hidden.title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts
articles_hidden.authors: Sandip Mishra, Payal, Declan Evans, Kingsley Bortey, Husayn Bootwala, Giovanni Gonzalez-Gutierrez, Ricardo Javier Vázquez, David Baker, Jared C. Lewis
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1–5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6–8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

articles_hidden.title: Drought and disease trigger novel interactions among top predators
articles_hidden.authors: Fabrizio Sergio, Haruki Natsukawa, Alessandro Tanferna, Javier Chicano, Francisco Carro, Ramón C. Soriguer, Fernando Hiraldo, Julio Blas
articles_hidden.abstract: Interactions among species are increasingly recognized as key determinants of climate change impacts on ecosystems 1–5 . However, we know little about how climatic perturbations affect interactions among top vertebrate predators. Here we show that, when an emergent disease caused the decline of shared prey (rabbits), after decades of neutral co-existence a mammalian carnivore (lynx) started to prey heavily on a top predatory raptor (kites). These predation bouts occurred exclusively under drought conditions and when lynx found rabbit remains under the raptor nests, consistent with the removal of a potential competitor. Drought-induced lynx predation depressed lifetime reproductive success and triggered territory abandonment and dispersal by the raptor, suggestive of a new arms race among predators. A reduction in raptor abundance was associated with an increase in an insectivorous bird (a small owl), showing that the new interaction had the potential to reach lower trophic levels. These results underline the importance of diet flexibility and mobility as important mediators of resilience to stressors. In the future, synergistic effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors may reshape the interactions and ecological roles of many apex predators, with potential cascading consequences for whole ecosystems. A key to forecasting the future impact of global change may reside in understanding how behavioural flexibility and interacting keystone species respond to interacting shocks.

Camilotti, Christiane Silvestrini, Filipe Loyola Lopes, Xin Lan, Gabrielle Pétron, Marcio Malacarne, Guilherme B. M. Machado
articles_hidden.abstract: The Amazon carbon sink is weakening as deforestation 1–5 , rising tree mortality 6–8 and climate change disrupt the climatic conditions that sustain a humid tropical forest 9–11 . Forest loss reduces precipitation, increases temperatures and lengthens the dry season, driving higher carbon emissions 1–4,11,12 . Climate stress is stronger in more deforested regions, rendering forests progressively more flammable 1,9,13 . Large-scale climate events, such as El Niño, further amplify regional climate impacts 9,14–17 . Here we present an analysis of 15 years of Amazonian carbon fluxes derived from atmospheric CO 2 measurements. We determine a carbon balance of 0.32 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 , with fires acting as the dominant source (0.40 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and forest uptake becoming increasingly unable to offset emissions. Furthermore, we investigate key drivers of the carbon emissions of Amazonia and identify three distinct year groups. Group 1 (2011–2014, 2017 and 2018) represents the role of the Amazon in the global carbon balance (0.11 ± 0.08 PgC yr −1 ) during wetter years with low human activity, such as deforestation, biomass burning and degradation. Group 2 (2019–2022) represents Amazon carbon emissions (0.43 ± 0.13 PgC yr −1 ) from human activities (mainly deforestation and degradation) during years with low climatic stress. Group 3 (2010, 2015, 2016, 2023 and 2024) has the highest carbon emissions (0.49 ± 0.07 PgC yr −1 ) and comprises warm and dry years (high climate stress), such as El Niño and the warming of the Tropical North Atlantic Ocean, associated with biomass burning.

articles_hidden.title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
articles_hidden.authors: Junsung Woo, Michael R. Williamson, Dongjoo Choi, Ekin Akdemir, Thea Zlatkov, Kwanha Yu, Wookbong Kwon, Ehson Maleki, Yeunjung Ko, Kaitlyn Sanchez, Hussein Maleki, Jong Min Choi, Akdes Serin-Harmanci, Benjamin Deneen
articles_hidden.abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes1,2. Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes3; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies4, we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51+ and CD51− astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51+ and CD51− astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51+ astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51+ astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51+ astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.

articles_hidden.title: Functional architecture of the human insula
articles_hidden.authors: Julian Quabs, Sofia Pantis, Guanpeng Chen, Weichen Huang, Eileen Ma, Maria del Vecchio, Dian Lyu, Chloe Wang, Pietro Avanzini, Vivek Buch, Ashwin G. Ramayya, Svenja Caspers, Hannes Vogel, Josef Parvizi
articles_hidden.abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7,8,9,10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal–posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral–posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior–polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

articles_hidden.title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation
articles_hidden.authors: Raphael P. H. Meier, Erwan Morgand, Fariza Mezine, Michael Mengel, Massimo Mangiola, Muhammad M. Mohiuddin, Robert A. Montgomery, Alexandre Loupy
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

articles_hidden.title: Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language
articles_hidden.authors: Fengyuan Dai, Shiyang You, Yudian Zhu, Yuan Gao, Lihao Fu, Xibin Zhou, Jin Su, Chentong Wang, Yuliang Fan, Qingsong Tan, Xiaoxiao Ma, Xianjun Deng, Letong Yu, Hui Qian, Yan He, Yitao Ke, Zhe Zhang, Chenchen Han, Xing Chang, Liangzhen Zheng, Sheng Wang, Yuan Ji, Kexin Hao, Longxing Cao, Yajie Wang, Anping Zeng, Shunzhi Wang, Chunjun Zhan, Jing Zhao, Tong Si, Jianming Liu, Hongyuan Lu, Fajie Yuan
articles_hidden.abstract: Programming biological function—designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks—is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1,2,3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein–text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks—a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein—and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.

articles_hidden.title: Touch-sensing digital pixel fibre enables interactive garment GUI
articles_hidden.authors: Heng Fu, Ziang Li, Swetika Chaturvedi, Xiaoyu Zhang, Xiaolong Li, Qianyi Li, Tural Khudiyev
articles_hidden.abstract: Wearable computing promises to transform human interaction with information, yet conventional graphical user interfaces (GUIs) rely on planar, rigid displays incompatible with textiles, which are composed of one-dimensional fibres. Despite recent progress1,2 in flexible and fibre-based displays, bridging this fundamental dimensional mismatch remains challenging because existing approaches do not naturally provide the digitally addressable, high-throughput, information-rich interfaces required for interactive GUIs. Here we present a digital pixel fibre integrating addressable pixels, a common propagation-axis interconnection for scalable in-fibre circuitry and a coaxial sensing layer for fibre-level touch localization. Microelectronic components and a touch-gated resistive path system form a linear circuit that acts as both an interactive display backbone and a computational bus, while peripheral multimodal fibre sensors and actuators enable physiological, inertial, optical, and acoustic input and output. We integrate these fibres into the forearm portion of a garment sleeve to realize a GUI with a 96 × 54-pixel display, 30-frame-per-second refresh rate and 8-bit colour depth. It supports dynamic graphics, integrated audio–video playback, wireless data exchange and interactive computing functions, while maintaining the flexibility, washability, breathability and mechanical robustness of everyday textiles. By merging display, sensing and computation within a single fibre, this work establishes a scalable platform for intrinsically interactive textiles, opening pathways toward garments that operate as fully integrated computational systems.

articles_hidden.title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
articles_hidden.authors: Pim W. J. M. Willemsen, Victoria G. Mason, Vincent van Zelst, Vera M. van Bergeijk, Mark Klein Breteler, Jos R. M. Muller, Dimitrios Dermentzoglou, Akis Vouziouris, Thomas J. van Veelen, S. Dzimballa, Kathelijne M. Wijnberg, Antonius J. F. Hoitink, Paul Buring, Maike Paul, Alessandro Antonini, Tjeerd J. Bouma, Bas W. Borsje
articles_hidden.abstract: Salt marshes protect coastlines by attenuating wind waves with their elevated marsh platform and above-ground vegetation1. Confidence in the persistence of this service under a changing climate requires knowledge on how extreme storms damage the platform and vegetation; however, a comprehensive, quantified understanding of salt marsh–wave interactions under extreme events is lacking. A unique experiment was conducted by transferring intact salt marsh to one of the world’s largest wave flumes, and subsequently exposing it to increasingly higher waves that reach up to 2 m significant wave height. We show that marsh substrates can persist with negligible erosion, despite cumulative wave exposure. By contrast, the vegetation was progressively damaged during continued wave exposure, gradually reducing vegetation-related wave attenuation. Results emphasize that vegetation was most effective in attenuating waves at low-energy marsh coasts (up to 1 m), where attenuation exceeded 10% (up to 50%), whereas attenuation at high-energy marsh coasts (wave height > 1 m) does not exceed 10%. Our global assessment supports the differentiation between low- and high-energetic conditions resulting from the flume experiment. Our results suggest that the marsh platform remains stable under extreme wave events and that substantial wave attenuation by marsh vegetation is limited to low-energy marsh coasts.

articles.title: Trait judgements of faces using a task without word labels
articles.authors: Yue Xu, Umit Keles, Chujun Lin, Ralph Adolphs
articles.abstract: People attribute psychological traits to faces. Previous research has typically elicited these judgements using specific words provided in advance by the experimenter (for example, ratings on competence or trustworthiness), raising questions about completeness (these tasks use a limited set of words) and generalizability (for example, across languages). Here we asked over 3,000 participants to spatially arrange unfamiliar faces based on perceived trait similarity, without providing any word labels. Using predominantly White faces, experiment 1 yielded five dimensions that we interpreted as approachability, gender-specific warmth, competence, morality and youthfulness. Using White, Black and Asian faces, experiment 2 also produced five dimensions, which showed prominent effects of stereotypes associated with race. Comparisons with four other studies that used word labels argue that approachability or warmth emerges as a universal evaluative factor that integrates multiple trait facets (such as trustworthiness, warmth and competence) into a single holistic dimension and that race and gender stereotypes emerge depending on the set of face stimuli used.

articles_hidden.title: Motor abstraction training generalizes to the refinement of specific movement patterns
articles_hidden.authors: Zekun Sun, Zhiran Xie, Samuel D. McDougle
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to abstract the invariant structure of an experience while discarding incidental details underlies generalization across virtually every domain of human cognition, from vision and language to concept learning. Yet whether the motor system generates such abstractions and whether they causally contribute to skilled performance remain open questions. Here we introduce a paradigm in which human participants learned novel movement patterns by precisely copying unfamiliar handwritten characters. To examine the role of motor abstractions in this form of learning, participants were trained on markedly rotated versions of the characters, which recruited substantially different lower-level movements while still maintaining the relevant abstract movement trajectory. Across 11 experiments, abstraction training drove robust performance improvements that were comparable to having repetitive practice on the canonical form of each character. Moreover, this effect was largely motoric in nature: it did not require a visual template, sustained trajectory feedback or mental imagery, and was sensitive to the sequential structure of the movement trajectory. These findings establish a causal role for abstractions in motor learning, revealing that the motor system probably deploys abstractions in the earliest stages of skill acquisition.

articles_hidden.title: Privileged representational axes in biological and artificial neural networks
articles_hidden.authors: Meenakshi Khosla, Sudhanshu Srivastava, Alex H. Williams, Josh McDermott, Nancy Kanwisher
articles_hidden.abstract: How do neurons code information? Recent work emphasizes the geometry and information content of population codes, using measures that are blind to the native tunings (or ‘axes’) of neural responses. But might these representational axes matter, with some privileged systematically over others? We developed methods to test for alignment of neural tuning across brains and deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). Across both vision and audition, both brains and DCNNs consistently favoured certain axes for representing the natural world. Moreover, the representational axes of DCNNs trained on natural inputs were aligned to those in perceptual cortices, such that axis-sensitive model–brain similarity metrics better differentiated competing models of biological sensory systems. We further show that coding schemes that privilege certain axes can facilitate task performance, reduce downstream wiring costs and improve generalization. These results motivate a new framework for understanding neural tuning in biological and artificial networks and its computational benefits.
