articles.title: Linguistic intervention unlocks the economic gains of diversity
articles.authors: Sheen S. Levine, Simon Siegenthaler, Bart J. Wilson
articles.abstract: Gains from trade generate prosperity, yet interpersonal exchange can falter along racial lines. We study incentivized experimental economies where participants must spontaneously initiate and sustain trading relationships with others whose race is visible. When the highest gains from trade require cross-race exchange, diverse economies underperform: welfare and specialization suffer as many retreat to autarky. This underperformance reflects not segregation into racial trading blocs, but a collapse in exchange. Opportunities for contact alone do not close the performance gap, which persists and even widens over time. To understand why, we turn to communication itself. Lower welfare is associated with less communication, fewer expressions of affiliation and achievement, and less explicit signaling of needs, deficits, and surpluses. We call this communicative misalignment: differences in shared-language use that raise search, bargaining, and coordination costs. A brief linguistic intervention equips participants with a communicative toolkit. It increases communication volume and the frequency of motivational and state-signaling language. Crucially, when gains depend on cross-race exchange, the intervention restores specialization and cross-race trade, closing the performance gap. Its effects are minimal when efficient trade need not cross race, indicating specificity rather than generic skill training. Language thus operates bidirectionally, both revealing the state of cooperation and causally shaping it. Although we examine racial boundaries, the mechanism may operate along other fault lines where interactional norms diverge, including hierarchy, geography, or culture. Language, a primary conduit of culture, can impede exchange when misaligned and facilitate it when aligned. This suggests a scalable micro-governance tool for reducing transaction costs.

articles.title: Scientists disrupt less but more persistently with career aging
articles.authors: Nan Deng, Liying Yang, Shlomo Havlin, An Zeng
articles.abstract: Disruption describes the extent to which a scientific work overturns the prior knowledge on which it builds and leads to a new line of research. A scientist’s tendency to produce disruptive work has been found recently to decline over the career. However, the disruption index captures only how strongly a paper overturns prior work and ignores whether that disruption is later accepted or overturned by subsequent research. The persistent disruption (PD) framework adds this second perspective, identifying work that disrupts prior research and is then consolidated rather than displaced by later work. We examine how PD evolves over the career and find the opposite pattern: The probability of producing a persistent disruptive paper increases with career age. Senior scientists disrupt prior work less often compared to young, but once they do, the disruption tends to persist rather than being quickly superseded. Our results suggest that this reversal feature is due to the experience and we corroborate it across several dimensions of recognition. We also show that, at a fixed level of disruptiveness, the more senior the scientist is, it attracts more citations, social-media attention, and research grants. Nobel laureates also show delayed persistent disruptions. They exhibit high disruptive ability early in their careers, yet their prize-winning work appears years later. This lag further indicates that experience is needed to turn disruptive ability into the field’s most celebrated contributions.

articles.title: Toward cooler cities by larger homogeneous functional clusters
articles.authors: Xucai Zhang, Xiaobing Wei, Xiaoping Liu, Honghong Wei, Yue Zheng, Hongkai Gu, Yangzi Che, Yeran Sun, Ming Luo, Weilin Liao, Haosheng Huang, Kangning Huang
articles.abstract: Urban heat island (UHI) intensifies heat-related risks and environmental degradation in cities worldwide, yet existing mitigation strategies have largely overlooked how the spatial scale of homogeneous functional building clusters influences local climate. This scale may matter because buildings with similar functions often share similar morphology, activity schedules, and anthropogenic heat-release patterns, allowing their spatial contiguity to shape ventilation and heat accumulation. Here, we introduce the Urban Homogeneous Scale (UHS)—an indicator that measures the spatial scale of contiguous, functionally similar building clusters—and analyze 233,844 observations across 101 global cities to assess its potential for mitigating surface UHI. We find that larger UHS is associated with lower surface UHI: every 100-meter increase in UHS corresponds to 4.5% decrease in daytime UHI. This daytime cooling effect is particularly more pronounced in inland, humid, and high-income regions. In low-income regions, larger building area and higher building volume more strongly weaken UHS cooling capacity than in wealthier regions, revealing a socioeconomic inequality in UHS’s mitigation benefits. Our findings identify the spatial scale of building clusters as a essential dimension of urban form associated with urban heat burden, and suggest that considering UHS alongside targeted controls on built environmental characteristics may inform future heat-mitigation planning.

articles.title: From authenticity ecosystems to human–AI hybrid societies
Education reduces dementia incidence and mitigates genetic risk
articles.authors: Silvia H. Barcellos, Leandro S. Carvalho, Kenneth M. Langa, Sneha Nimmagadda, Patrick Turley
articles.abstract: There is little causal evidence on factors that can protect individuals against Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) risk. We study the causal effect of education on ADRD, exploiting a regression discontinuity generated by a compulsory schooling reform. ADRD was ascertained based on medical history, hospital records, and death registries, addressing concerns about selective sample attrition. We find that education reduces incidence of ADRD. Using molecular genetic data, we show that the reform weakened the relationship between genetics and ADRD incidence, implying genetic risk of dementia is not immutable and can be modified by social policy.

articles.title: Diminishing cooling returns of urban greening amid a warming climate
articles.authors: Song Leng, Hongbin He, Alfredo Huete, Ekena Rangel Pinagé, Wenjie Zhang, Honghao Ding, Liding Chen, Ranhao Sun
articles.abstract: Urban greening is widely prioritized as a nature-based solution to mitigating intensifying heat extremes in the context of climate change, yet its long-term global efficacy remains inadequately quantified. Here we present a two-decade assessment of vegetation dynamics and associated cooling effects across 3,806 urban clusters worldwide, integrating multisource satellite observations with ground measurements from 4,855 meteorological stations. We identify a pronounced climate equity gap: While cities in the Global North have largely expanded green infrastructure, they exhibit cooling saturation with diminishing biophysical returns. Conversely, most cities in the Global South show vegetation stagnation or loss, compounding rapid warming trends. This asymmetry exposes a critical climate justice challenge, indicating that current greening efforts are insufficient to offset a warming trend. Our findings underscore the necessity for context-specific, integrated climate adaptation frameworks that address both the quantity and quality of urban vegetation to achieve equitable thermal resilience in an increasingly warm world.

articles_hidden.title: A functional two-pore-domain K + channel from a large DNA virus
articles_hidden.authors: Oliver Rauh, Sebastian Mach, Oliver Clarke, Jonas Toews, James L. Van Etten, Mike Althaus, Anna Moroni, Gerhard Thiel
articles_hidden.abstract: The evolutionary history of proteins helps to understand their structure/function correlates and suggests on how functional complexity evolved from primitive precursors. In the superfamily of K + channels, functional features of complex eukaryotic inward rectifier (Kir) channels and voltage-dependent (Kv) channels could be understood in terms of an increase in structural complexity of their prokaryotic precursors. K2P channels, which are made from tandem repeats of two pore domains, are not found in prokaryotes and their evolutionary origin is still unknown. In searching for primitive K2P channel precursors, we screened the genomes of nucleocytoplasmic large DNA viruses (NCLDVs) for genes coding for K2P channels. This was motivated by two reasons: NCLDVs are already known for coding primitive Kir type channels, and they play important roles in the evolution of eukaryotes. Here, we report that the NCLDV Pyramimonas orientalis virus codes for K2P-like K + channels. With only 178 amino acids and no cytosolic domains, this Kpov protein is much smaller than any eukaryotic K2P channel, but still functional as K + selective channel in lipid bilayers. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that Kpov is not the product of molecular piracy from the host but may result from fusion of primitive viral K + channel pore domains.

articles_hidden.title: Signal peptides for engineered protein secretion by free and hydrogel-encapsulated cyanobacteria
articles_hidden.authors: Nathan T. Soulier, Debika Datta, Rakefet Schwarz, Jonathan K. Pokorski, James W. Golden, Susan S. Golden
articles_hidden.abstract: Cyanobacteria provide a promising platform for light-driven heterologous protein production. In heterologous production systems, cells are typically lysed for product purification or to facilitate interaction with external substrates, unless the product is secreted. Fusion to molecular “shipping labels” known as signal peptides can target chimeric proteins to native membrane translocation pathways and result in secretion. In this work, we identified signal peptides from the model cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus PCC 7942 ( S. elongatus ) and genetically fused to two heterologous enzymes: the reporter nanoluciferase (NLuc) and an oxidative laccase (CotA). Increased extracellular activity was observed for one or more signal-protein variants for both enzymes. Furthermore, cells of S. elongatus producing a signal-laccase chimera were encapsulated within an alginate hydrogel, and the resulting engineered living material released sufficient enzyme to decolorize a dye pollutant in its surroundings. These findings streamline recombinant protein production in cyanobacteria and facilitate environmental interactions with cell products, expanding the potential applications of both free-living and material-encapsulated cyanobacteria.

articles_hidden.title: Understory diversity is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration
articles_hidden.authors: Yakun Zhang, Rui Zhang, Scott X. Chang, Han Y. H. Chen, Anthony R. Taylor, Masumi Hisano, Chen Chen, Sai Peng, Ya Wang, Xin Chen, Jiasheng Wu, Xinli Chen, Peter B. Reich
articles_hidden.abstract: Forests are a major terrestrial carbon sink, and higher overstory diversity is often associated with greater carbon accrual in trees and soils. Yet the contribution of the understory vegetation, the most species-rich forest stratum, to tree and soil carbon accumulation remains largely unknown. Here, we analyzed Canada’s National Forest Inventory database to explore whether understory diversity (richness and evenness of shrubs, herbs, and bryophytes) is associated with carbon accumulation in overstory trees and soils across environmental gradients of air temperature, climate moisture, and nitrogen deposition. We found that herb and bryophyte species richness were positively associated with decadal tree carbon accumulation, with the strongest effects at warmer, drier, and nitrogen-limited sites. In contrast, understory diversity showed no consistent association with soil carbon accumulation. On a decadal scale, increasing herb and bryophyte species richness from their minimum to median values corresponded to 15% and 6% increases in tree carbon accumulation, respectively. These results provide large-scale observational evidence that diversity in lower vegetation layers is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration and reveal strong environmental modulation of these multistratal biodiversity–ecosystem functioning relationships. These findings suggest that species-rich herb and bryophyte communities should be considered in strategies for sustaining forest carbon sinks, especially under warmer, drier conditions and nutrient limitation.

articles_hidden.title: Biotic response networks are an important organizer of the transcriptome in wild Arabidopsis thaliana populations
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Paula Leite Montalvão, Kevin D. Murray, Ilja Bezrukov, Natalie Betz, Lucas P. Henry, Paloma Duran, Patrick Boppert, Martina Kolb, NA, Fabrice Roux, Joy Bergelson, Detlef Weigel, Wei Yuan, Haim Ashkenazy, Tien-Hao Chang, Choghag Demijirian, Rémi Duflos, Alejandra Duque-Jaramillo, Katrin Fritschi, Andrew Gloss, Anette Habring, Katharina Klein, Eric Laderman, Irene Leccia, Roxane Lion, Hanna Märkle, Baptiste Mayjonade, Timothy C. Morton, Ankita Pandey, Alexandre Perrat, Kamal Radharamanan, Angelique Rat, Sonia Silva, Manmeet Singh, Daniel de Souza, Hannah Whitehurst
articles_hidden.abstract: Extensive laboratory experimentation has revealed conserved molecular pathways controlling growth and stress responses in plants, yet how these programs operate in natural settings remains poorly understood. We have investigated the organization of the transcriptome in wild populations of Arabidopsis thaliana by sampling plants across 60 natural sites in Europe and North America over two seasons. Transcriptomes varied extensively among individuals and were only weakly structured by geography or season. No groups of plants stood out due to clear biotic or abiotic stress signatures known from the laboratory. While only a small portion of transcriptome variance was explained by disease symptoms or environmental and phenotypic variables, infection-associated signals accounted for the largest share of the explainable fraction. Biotic-response networks identified in controlled laboratory conditions were well conserved in wild transcriptomes, while other networks, including abiotic-response networks were substantially reorganized in wild plants. Together, these results indicate that while certain transcriptional modules are easily reidentified when moving from the wild to controlled conditions, many regulatory relationships differ in these two contexts, highlighting how ecological complexity shapes transcriptome organization in natural populations.

articles_hidden.title: Bridging spatial scales in respiratory viral infection
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrik Hvid, Bjarke Frost Nielsen, Kim Sneppen
articles_hidden.abstract: Respiratory viruses spread within the host through a combination of local expansion and occasional long-range dissemination that seeds new infection foci. We present LEAP (Lotka-Euler Airway Pathogen model), an analytically tractable within-host model that captures this two-scale process. The model takes the form of an age-dependent branching process and yields a closed-form expression for the exponential growth rate during early infection. Using empirical data to parameterize the model, we find that productive dissemination requires only a small number of successful long-range seeding events per infected cell, with distinct values for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus. LEAP further predicts that, in these well-adapted viruses, interferon-mediated restriction only weakly affects exponential growth, while remaining decisive for poorly adapted pathogens. More broadly, the model provides a flexible framework for experimentally testable predictions of early infection dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: The survival paradox of close-in planets orbiting red-clump giants
articles_hidden.authors: Wen-Xu Lin, Sheng-Bang Qian, Qi-Bin Sun, Li-Ying Zhu, Wen-Ping Liao, Ting Li, Fu-Xing Li, Xiang-Dong Shi, Tao Wang, Er-Gang Zhao, Hui-Ting Zhang, Ping Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Close-in planets orbiting core-helium-burning red-clump giants directly challenge tidal-engulfment theory, which predicts that planets within about 1 au of Sun-like stars should be engulfed during red-giant-branch (RGB) expansion. The existence of such survivors would imply missing physical processes in the late stages of stellar and planetary evolution. Yet only one such “forbidden” planet had been identified to date. Here we report three systems—24 Boo b, HD 12648 b, and TYC 4282-605-1 b—whose host stars are confirmed red-clump giants through asteroseismology, showing that each has already undergone dramatic expansion and contraction following helium ignition. Their planets now reside at orbital separations smaller than the maximum stellar radii attained during the RGB phase, implying that they should not have survived. Among them, 24 Boo b orbits at only 0.183 au with a 30-d period, making it the closest planet known around a red-clump giant. These findings demonstrate that this paradox is not an isolated anomaly but signals the emergence of a class of evolved planetary systems. Their survival defies current models of stellar–planetary coevolution and points to unexplored physics shaping planetary architectures around post-RGB stars.

articles_hidden.title: Molecular fossils of an ancestral code revealed by large-scale analysis of tRNAs
articles_hidden.authors: Ash Nova Royo, Paula Martín-Cabezas, Sergey Ovchinnikov, Paul Schimmel, Lluís Ribas de Pouplana
articles_hidden.abstract: Modern tRNAs are thought to have evolved from simpler RNA minihelices resembling acceptor stems, some of which could be specifically aminoacylated. A central and testable prediction of minihelix-based models is that vestiges of ancestral coding relationships should remain embedded within the acceptor stems of contemporary tRNAs and should persist after correction for structural constraints. Here, we ask whether cognate anticodon-like triplets are statistically enriched in nonanticodon regions of modern tRNAs beyond what would be expected from structural and compositional constraints alone. Using a curated dataset of 77,335 canonical tRNA sequences and a structure-aware statistical framework, we find that for a subset of amino acids cognate anticodon-like triplets are significantly enriched in acceptor stems and, to a lesser extent, in other structural domains. Notably, these amino acids include those previously shown to support specific minihelix aminoacylation [Y. M. Hou, P. Schimmel, Nature 333 , 140–145 (1988); C. Francklyn, P. Schimmel, Nature 337 , 478–481 (1989)]. The strongest acceptor-stem signals survive structure-preserving null models, and cluster nonrandomly against proposed chronologies of amino acid incorporation into the genetic code. Together, these findings identify molecular fossils within modern tRNAs consistent with the persistence of an ancestral operational code, and provide refined statistical support for the notion that extant codon–amino acid relationships evolved from early aminoacylation systems involving RNA minihelices.

articles_hidden.title: Reduction of aflatoxin contamination in maize kernels mediated by host-induced gene silencing
articles_hidden.authors: Ali Ahmed, Keri Cavanaugh, Patricia Baldrich, Ioannis Stergiopoulos, Richard Michelmore
articles_hidden.abstract: Aflatoxins produced by some species of Aspergillus pose a significant threat to global food safety, because they contaminate a variety of crops including maize. In this study, we used host-induced gene silencing (HIGS) to reduce aflatoxin accumulation in maize upon infection with Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus . Two RNAi constructs were designed and introduced into maize, one targeting two essential fungal genes involved in ergosterol biosynthesis ( CYP51A and CYP51B ) and the other targeting three aflatoxin biosynthesis genes ( AflC , AflD , and AflR ). The presence of RNAi transgenes was confirmed in 17 and 14 independent lines possessing the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi construct and the AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi construct, respectively. Most transgenic lines had single-locus integrations and one or two copies of the transgene. Transgene expression varied considerably among the lines. Small RNA sequencing confirmed the production of siRNAs from the HIGS trigger sequences. Levels of CYP51A , AflC , AflD, and AflR transcripts in Aspergillus spp. were successfully decreased upon infection of transgenic maize. However, significant reduction in the level of CYP51B transcripts was not achieved and the CYP51A/CYP51B RNAi transgene had no discernible effect on fungal growth in infected maize. In contrast, we observed significant reductions in aflatoxin accumulation in four AflC/AflD/AflR RNAi transgenic lines infected with A. flavus and in two transgenic lines infected with A. parasiticus . Notably, one AflC/AflD/AflR transgenic line exhibited minimal aflatoxin contamination upon kernel infection with A. parasiticus . These results demonstrate the potential of HIGS to reduce aflatoxin production in mature corn kernels.

articles_hidden.title: Capillary physics links HIV capsid geometry to nuclear pore translocation
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander W. Brown, Sami C. Al-Izzi, Jack L. Parker, Sophie Hertel, David A. Jacques, Halim Kusumaatmaja, Richard G. Morris
articles_hidden.abstract: The protective capsid encasing the genetic material of HIV can traverse the nuclear pore complex (NPC) intact, despite being far larger than conventional passive cargo. This is attributed to the properties of the capsid surface, which promote partitioning into cohesive assemblies of the disordered proteins that form the NPC’s permeability barrier: phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins (FG-Nups). The implication, at the mesoscale, is that capsid–NPC interactions are characterized by the interfacial physics of wetting and capillarity. To capture this, we develop a minimal theory that reduces to an interplay between capsid geometry, effective cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic contact angles, and a ratio of interfacial tensions. By combining analytical calculations, sharp- and diffuse-interface numerics, we make several predictions: A geometry-dependent trade-off between penetration depth and the wetting transition; asymmetric capillary forces that generate torques and lead to metastable “stalled” states that are tilted; a topological classification of the possible mechanisms underlying the largest energetic barrier; and spontaneous symmetry breaking of displaced FG-Nups. These behaviors connect capsid shape and orientation to the topology and symmetry of FG-Nup displacement, and to the molecular compositions on each side of the pore. They are consistent with published cryoelectron tomography orientations, which provide an initial estimate of the cytoplasmic contact angle. Crucially, our results identify a capillary advantage for the HIV capsid’s characteristic broken-symmetry geometry.

articles_hidden.title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models
articles_hidden.authors: Mina Cullen, Carmen Biancaniello, Katerina Taškova, Vedran Miletić, Alfonso De Simone, Davide Mercadante
articles_hidden.abstract: With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from C α -only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to explore phenomena such as secondary structure propensity and nucleation in condensates, conformationally selected binding motifs across disordered ensembles or conformational preferences of sequence-specific short-linear motifs.

articles_hidden.title: The susceptibility to weight gain in male C57BL/6 mice fed high-fat diet is due to a small set of genes predominantly not expressed in the brain
articles_hidden.authors: Yingga Wu, Agata M. Rudolf, Lu Wang, Zhengjie Zhang, Chaoqun Niu, Fan Xia, Min Li, Anyongqi Wang, Davina Derous, Sharon E. Mitchell, Haoran Zhang, Yalin He, John R. Speakman
articles_hidden.abstract: Obesity results from a gene by environment interaction. Understanding the impacts of environmental factors like diet on body weight/fatness has been greatly facilitated by rodent models. We previously identified the responses of males of five mouse strains fed 30 different diets. Two of these strains showed much greater weight gain and two were resistant. Sixty-six marker SNPs in 57 genes were identified, which have a genetic motif across the four strains reflecting their protection or susceptibility to high-fat diet (HFD). We used two of these strains: C57BL/6 and BALB/c, in a classic approach of cross-breeding the strains, to generate a F1 generation, and then cross-breeding their offspring to generate an F2 population. The F2 males were fed HFD and phenotyped for body weight, fat mass, and energy intake and genotyped for the 66 SNPs. Body mass gain on HFD was influenced by 17 SNPs in 11 genes explaining 87% of the individual variation in weight gain. We then measured gene expression of these 11 genes in 16 tissues of male and female C57BL/6 and Balb/c mice when fed high- or low-fat diets, and in 6 tissues of mice exposed to different levels of calorie restriction, to map their expression profiles. The genes were widely expressed in a diversity of tissues including several not normally suspected to be important for fat storage regulation (e.g., testis, lungs, and spleen) with only four expressed predominantly in the hypothalamus. Body fat regulation is probably more complex than current models focused on the brain–adipose axis suppose.

articles_hidden.title: Screw dislocation–mediated galaxy-mimicking superspiral assembly with amplified bio-piezoelectricity
articles_hidden.authors: Jiahao Zhang, Haoran Wu, Shixuan Xu, Haoye Jiang, Kang Ma, Syed A. M. Tofail, Deqing Mei, Junbai Li, Kai Tao
articles_hidden.abstract: From the galaxies to the petals, spiral architectures are ubiquitous to confer hierarchical organizations, supporting asymmetric galactic evolutions and biological activities. Herein, inspired from nature, we report the superspiral architectures self-assembled by a minimalist amino acid. These superspirals, with spirality and geometry programmably tuned by enantiomeric excess and organization parameters, are determined to arise from the screw dislocation induced hierarchical crystallization. Notably, the spiral organization can integrate and amplify electrical polarization, yielding 17-fold enhancement in piezoelectric response contrast to random aggregates. This allows engineering of piezoelectric bioelectronics, resulting in high gain direction-selective motion sensing. Our work establishes an alternative paradigm for developing bioinspired hierarchical architectures of oriented and amplified properties, offering a self-assembling route to explore programmably modulated functional architectures for bioelectronic engineering.

articles_hidden.title: Magnetically guided programmable thermomechanical protection enabled by biomimetic asymmetric design
articles_hidden.authors: Zimu Li, Jianfeng Huang, Sheng Wang, Jianpeng Wu, Shuai Liu, Zhihao Hu, Guilin Mei, Xinglong Gong
articles_hidden.abstract: Precision instruments operating in harsh environments require protective materials that can dissipate impact energy while resisting heat. However, actively tunable thermomechanical protection under coupled multiphysics conditions remains challenging. Inspired by shellfish and echinoderms, here we show that an asymmetrically engineered shear-stiffening gel (SSG) yields a Janus magnetorheological elastomer whose two faces mimic the brick-and-mortar architecture of shellfish and the impact-hardening behavior of echinoderms, respectively. Unlike single-modification anti-creep strategies of SSG that degrade shear-stiffening or severely increase initial modulus, our design achieves a 40-fold mechanical tunability, with the storage modulus ranging from 11.29 to 450.28 kPa, arising from the synergistic enhancement of strain-rate-dependent stiffening and magnetic interactions. The integration of magnetic and optical functions enables semiactive noncontact 2D-to-3D protection, achieving an 85% reduction in impact force and a 40 °C temperature difference via bidirectional photothermal regulation, demonstrating competitive thermomechanical protection performance. Furthermore, this strategy establishes a magnetically guided programmable pathway for thermomechanical protection and provides a generalizable blueprint for multifunctional intelligent materials, advancing protective technologies for outdoor equipment operating in extreme environments involving coupled physical fields.

articles_hidden.title: Translational control of microglial metabolism, inflammatory responses, and survival by the eIF4E-binding proteins
articles_hidden.authors: Sara Bermudez, Jung-Hyun Choi, Niaz Mahmood, Jacob W. Vogel, Hashem Almousa, Ziying Huang, Sung-Hoon Kim, Vivian Yuchan Zhu, Linqiao Zhou, Diana Casas-Antillon, Moein Yaqubi, Danielle Cozachenco, Jo Anne Stratton, Oskar Hansson, Luke Healy, Argel Aguilar-Valles, Nahum Sonenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes microglial neuroprotective functions by engaging multiple cell receptors. However, the relevant downstream effectors are not fully understood. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) promotes mRNA translation by phosphorylating and inactivating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 and 2 (4E-BP1/2), which are expressed in microglia. 4E-BP1 levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in AD and correlate with markers of microglial reactivity and disease progression. Using linear regression analysis, we found that elevated CSF 4E-BP1 levels strengthen the association between soluble TREM2 levels and neurodegeneration in amyloid-positive individuals. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we performed in vitro experiments demonstrating that amyloid-β inactivated 4E-BP1 in murine microglia. The mTOR-mediated inactivation is highly dependent on Spleen Tyrosine Kinase (SYK) signaling and repeated exposure to amyloid-β impaired this process, whereas prolonged exposure increased 4E-BP1 levels in microglia. Deletion of 4E-BP1/2 resulted in increased mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation, reduced pro-inflammatory signaling, and protected microglia from amyloid-induced apoptosis. Thus, impaired 4E-BP1 inactivation—due to reduced mTOR signaling or excess 4E-BP1—disrupts immune resolution, leading to metabolic exhaustion and microglial cell death. We identify the SYK–mTORC1–4E-BP1 signaling axis as a key regulator of microglial mitochondrial biogenesis and immune resolution in AD.

articles_hidden.title: Catalytic reactive-hydrogen membranes for rapid capture and hydrodefluorination of six PFAS of regulatory concern
articles_hidden.authors: Min Long, Ai-Shi Wang, Welman C. Elias, Chen Zhou, Thomas P. Senftle, Michael S. Wong, Jie Cheng, Bruce E. Rittmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) persist in aquatic environments due to their ultrastable C–F bonds and poor susceptibility to conventional treatment. Here, we report an H 2 -based catalytic-film membrane that enables PFAS destruction in ambient conditions by generating highly reactive surface (H ads * ) and subsurface hydrogen (H sub * ), the latter stored as β-phase palladium hydride (β-PdHx). Solid-state analyses evidenced β-PdHx formation and related lattice expansion with elevated H 2 chemical potential, revealing a structural mechanism that links hydrogen storage to catalytic defluorination. Mechanistically, the two hydrogen species play complementary roles: H ads * -rich Pd 0 surface enabled PFAS capture through parallel adsorption to maximize interfacial contact with active H, whereas sustained H sub * supplied the energetic driving force for stepwise hydrodefluorination consistent with sequential C–F scission. As a result, across six PFAS of regulatory concern—PFOA, PFOS, PFNA, PFHxS, PFBS, and GenX—the catalytic membrane converted all contaminants toward fully defluorinated products. Long-chain PFAS were removed and defluorinated more rapidly than short-chain analogs, while GenX showed greater recalcitrance due to its ether linkage, weaker adsorption, and higher average C–F bond dissociation energy; nonetheless, GenX still exhibited removal and defluorination, with the production of 2-propoxypropanoic acid. The system also enabled continuous coremoval of all six PFAS in ambient conditions, with up to 96% removal and 83% defluorination over 58 d. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for how active hydrogen is generated, stored, and deployed in catalytic membranes, and identify engineered H 2 -catalytic membranes as a promising low-energy technology for destructive PFAS treatment.

articles_hidden.title: Multiple sources contribute to predictive tactile attenuation in the mouse whisker system
articles_hidden.authors: Kalpana Gupta, Shubhodeep Chakrabarti, Cornelius Schwarz
articles_hidden.abstract: The brain predicts action outcomes using interacting neuronal systems that integrate sensory feedback, movement, and rewards. In the mouse whisker system, we investigated whether two presumed predictive mechanisms jointly attenuate ascending tactile signals during movement. To this end, we employed an open-loop whisker-reach task that monitored facial nucleus motor activity and presented experimental tactile consequences while measuring tactile attenuation in the barrel cortex. Experimentally manipulating sensory consequences revealed two distinct systems. Sensory gating, a previously documented but functionally unclear mechanism of tactile attenuation, appeared graded but persisted during and after movement. In contrast, a second system was found to be temporally precise, generate suppression when stimuli are omitted, and capable of being learned within hundreds of trials. We label it state estimation as its characteristics—active suppression of expected tactile input—aligns well with the classical reafference principle, previously overlooked in the whisker system.

articles_hidden.title: Validation of targets linked to weight gain in C57BL/6 mice and translational aspects in humans
articles_hidden.authors: Yingga Wu, Agata M. Rudolf, Lu Wang, Zhengjie Zhang, Chaoqun Niu, Fan Xia, Min Li, Anyongqi Wang, Sharon E. Mitchell, Haoran Zhang, Yalin He, Chunyu Chen, John R. Speakman
articles_hidden.abstract: Obesity is linked to complex interactions between an organism’s genetic background and its environment. Mouse models have been invaluable research tools to study obesity, with C57BL/6N being widely studied, given its propensity for weight gain on a high-fat diet (HFD). Despite this, the genetic basis of its susceptibility is poorly understood. In a partner paper we have identified SNP variants in 11 genes causing susceptibility to, or protection against, HFD-induced obesity in male C57BL/6N mice explaining 87% of the individual variation in fat gain. Surprisingly, most of them were maximally expressed outside the brain. In this study, we further validate some of these targets. We demonstrate that tissue-specific inhibition of Nova1 and Mchr1 in muscle, Nr1i3 in liver, and Ahr in lung and liver led to resistance to HFD–induced obesity or glucose intolerance. Further RNAseq analysis revealed that mTOR, Acox1, IL-15, and eIF2a signals are positioned downstream of these genes, potentially mediating their effects on obesity susceptibility. Importantly, variants in eight of the genes identified here have been previously implicated in human obesity, suggesting that a deeper understanding of the genetic/environment interactions of model systems can inform this complex human disease. Our work confirms that body fat regulation is likely more complex than current models which focus on the brain–adipose axis suggest.

articles_hidden.title: Calibration, accuracy, and domain variation across one million collective forecasts from prediction platforms
articles_hidden.authors: Justin Dickerson, Hilla Shinitzky, Maayan Peer, Mattan S. Ben-Shachar, Michael Gilead
articles_hidden.abstract: Using approximately one million resolved contracts and questions across four collective forecasting platforms, twelve domains, and time horizons ranging from hours to years, we evaluate the calibration and accuracy of collective forecasts in real-world settings. We found that forecast probabilities were overall highly calibrated: events assigned a probability of p % occurred approximately p % of the time. This broad pattern was evident across platforms and many domains, although fine-grained analyses revealed systematic tendencies toward over- or underestimation in highly consequential areas. While this does not mean that forecasting platforms provide certainty about individual events, our findings suggest that large-scale aggregation of judgments contains meaningful information about real-world uncertainty; when examined in aggregate, the predictions generated by the platforms provided informative estimates of event likelihood.

articles_hidden.title: Virus transmission required for maintenance and host adaptation mirrors neurophysiological differences in rabies-derived peptides
articles_hidden.authors: Alice Remal, Emily S. Acheson, Patrick A. Leighton, Erin E. Rees, John Rhodes, Brittany C. V. O’Brien, Maegan M. Weltzin, Karsten Hueffer
articles_hidden.abstract: Pathogen adaptations to new hosts are central to the disease ecology of cross-species transmission and host switching of viruses. The rabies virus is a model for adaptations to different hosts as it induces behavioral changes that facilitate transmission, while being maintained in distinct species-specific cycles of infection. Here, we demonstrate that the rabies virus requires distinct transmission dynamics in two hosts with different ecologies to establish maintenance, using agent-based modeling, analyses of virus glycoprotein-mediated manipulation of neuroreceptor function, and phylogenetic analysis. Epidemiological models suggest that rabies virus variants adapted to arctic foxes, which sustain rabies virus at very low host densities, require a higher probability of transmission than viruses adapted to raccoons. Using in vitro electrophysiology, we demonstrate that the rabies glycoprotein-derived peptides from arctic fox rabies variants are more potent antagonists of alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. These findings suggest a possible functional basis for the behavioral modifications that drive enzootic rabies transmission in the context of host ecology. In addition, a large proportion of residues that may drive rabies virus adaptation to raccoons and arctic foxes are found within this neurotoxin-like region. Furthermore, a residue in the neurotoxin-like region of the mature rabies virus glycoprotein (residue 183) has been associated with pathogenicity, host switching, and disease ecology in previous studies. We propose the hypothesis that rabies virus transmission dynamics adapt to the ecology and physiology of novel hosts through the selection of glycoproteins that elicit specific degrees of behavioral modification and transmission probability.

articles_hidden.title: A tunable immune-evasion function of Zika virus NS5 governs viral fitness and pathogenesis
articles_hidden.authors: Yu Zhang, Yaqing Zhang, Chengyu Liu, Wenlin Ren, Yu Zhao, Chenhao Li, Yongqi Guo, Leyi Bai, Peigang Wang, Jing An, Jun Liu, Qiang Ding
articles_hidden.abstract: Type I interferon (IFN) signaling is a central antiviral defense, with STAT2 driving the expression of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) to restrict viral infection. Zika virus (ZIKV) and dengue virus evade this pathway through nonstructural protein 5 (NS5)-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of STAT2, yet the contribution of this immune-evasion strategy to viral fitness and pathogenesis remains incompletely defined. Here, using a multistep mutational scanning strategy that jointly assessed STAT2 degradation and viral RNA replication, we identified a single NS5 residue, L162, as uniquely permissive to substitution that abolishes STAT2 degradation without compromising intrinsic replication functions. Substitution of L162 with alanine or glycine (L162A or L162G) selectively disrupted NS5 recruitment of the ZSWIM8-CUL3 E3 ubiquitin ligase, thereby preserving STAT2 stability and restoring IFN signaling. Recombinant ZIKV carrying these mutations exhibited reduced replication and enhanced ISG induction in human cells, defects fully rescued by STAT2 knockout. In A129 mice (type I IFN receptor deficient), mutant and WT viruses replicated comparably, but in human STAT2 knock-in mice, ZIKV-NS5 L162G exhibited markedly reduced viral loads and disease. In pregnant human STAT2 knock-in mice, the mutant also reduced placental and fetal viral burdens and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Notably, infection with ZIKV-NS5 L162G elicited robust neutralizing antibody and T cell responses that conferred protection against WT challenge. Together, these findings establish NS5-mediated STAT2 degradation as a central determinant of ZIKV immune-evasion, viral fitness, and pathogenesis and highlight disruption of NS5–STAT2 antagonism as a promising strategy for antiviral intervention and rational attenuation.

articles_hidden.title: Widespread plasma jets in the Martian magnetosheath revealed by dual-spacecraft observations
articles_hidden.authors: Abigail Tadlock, Chuanfei Dong, Chi Zhang, Savvas Raptis, Hongyang Zhou, Xinmin Li, Jiawei Gao
articles_hidden.abstract: Plasma jets in planetary magnetosheaths are transient, high dynamic pressure structures capable of strongly perturbing downstream magnetospheres and modulating solar wind energy transfer. Although recently identified at Mars, their formation mechanisms and global occurrence remain poorly constrained. Using dual-spacecraft observations from Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN and Tianwen-1, we show that magnetosheath jets occur throughout the Martian magnetosheath, in striking contrast to Earth where jet occurrence is strongly controlled by interplanetary magnetic field orientation and largely confined to quasi-parallel shock regions. We propose that this widespread distribution is linked to Mars’ extended hydrogen corona, which generates pickup ions that drive proton-cyclotron waves upstream of the bow shock. Because this mechanism is generic to any body with an extended corona (or exosphere) embedded in a stellar wind, this finding bears on solar–wind interactions at comets and other small bodies, and on the space environments of unmagnetized terrestrial exoplanets. These results indicate that magnetosheath jet formation can be governed not only by external solar wind forcing but also by intrinsic planetary properties, pointing to a previously unrecognized pathway for solar wind–planet coupling at unmagnetized worlds.

articles_hidden.title: Structure of a sparsely populated chimeric intermediate that facilitates fold-switching of a metamorphic protein
articles_hidden.authors: Bodhisatwa Nandi, Ashok Sekhar
articles_hidden.abstract: Metamorphic proteins challenge the single-sequence-structure-function paradigm by switching between distinct folds that often adopt complementary functions. However, the conformational states sampled along the fold-switching pathway have remained elusive because they are transient and unstable. Using multinuclear chemical exchange saturation transfer and relaxation dispersion NMR, combined with chemical shift–based structure determination and protein engineering, we visualized the atomic resolution structure of an “invisible” state of the metamorphic chemokine lymphotactin. This state is a chimera that integrates the secondary and tertiary structure of one fold with the quaternary assembly of the other. Locking lymphotactin into a single conformation abolishes access to this state, supporting its role as an on-pathway intermediate in metamorphosis. The stabilization of such hybrid intermediates is likely to have facilitated the evolution of fold-switching and represents a powerful strategy for protein design.

articles_hidden.title: Mitochondrial subpopulations promote cellular responses to changes in metabolic demand and signal transduction
articles_hidden.authors: Tak Shun Fung, Elias Tzoc-Pacheco, Ruobing Cui, Shelby Brown, Simon Schwörer, Tullia Lindsten, Craig B. Thompson, Keunwoo Ryu
articles_hidden.abstract: When mammalian cells are under increased ATP demand, mitochondria segregate into two distinct subpopulations, one capable of oxidative phosphorylation (oxidative subpopulation) and another specialized in reductive synthesis of metabolic precursors (reductive subpopulation). Here we report that mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) along with protein components of the mitochondrial nucleoid segregate to the oxidative subpopulation in response to increased ATP demand. This suggests that formation of the reductive mitochondrial subpopulation might serve to eliminate alternative uses of mitochondrial NAD(P)H when cells are under bioenergetic or nutrient stress. To examine this further, we studied mitochondria in cells exposed to low levels of glutamine. Mitochondria use glutaminase (GLS1) to maintain net glutamine uptake when cytosolic glutamine decreases, by converting glutamine to glutamate. The resulting glutamate can either be oxidized into α-ketoglutarate to enter the TCA cycle or utilized in the reductive synthesis of proline/ornithine. GLS1 can polymerize into hyperactive filaments in response to elevations in inorganic phosphate as might occur when ATP consumption exceeds production. However, when extracellular glutamine is reduced, GLS1 filaments segregated away from mtDNA, becoming colocalized with pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS) filaments in reductive mitochondria lacking ATP synthase markers. This cosegregation supported the ability of TGF-β signaling to enhance reductive proline/ornithine biosynthesis under low glutamine conditions despite compromising oxidative TCA cycle support from glutamine. The cosegregation of GLS1-P5CS filaments depended on continuing mitochondrial fission/fusion and occurred even in cells lacking mtDNA. Together, these data demonstrate that the reductive mitochondrial subpopulation is functional and under regulation by both metabolic demand and intercellular signal transduction.

articles_hidden.title: Gene conversion is a key driver of diversity hotspots in Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens and virulence-associated loci
articles_hidden.authors: Maximillian G. Marin, Natalia Quinones-Olvera, Hu Jin, Michael A. Harris, Brendan M. Jeffrey, Alex Rosenthal, Kenan C. Murphy, Christopher M. Sassetti, Heng Li, Maha R. Farhat
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite the long-held view of Mycobacterium tuberculosis ( Mtb ) as a genetically conserved pathogen, many genomic regions remain poorly resolved due to high sequence homology and repetitive content. Using complete genome assemblies generated from long-read sequencing of 151 globally representative clinical isolates, we comprehensively analyzed genome-wide patterns of genetic diversity and evolution across the Mtb genome. Our analysis uncovers pronounced diversity hotspots within paralogous regions (PRs) generated by recurrent gene conversion between homologous genes. In many cases, these hotspots exhibit more than an order of magnitude greater genetic diversity than the rest of the Mtb genome, which is otherwise characterized by remarkably low variation. Mutations within these regions display clustered substitution patterns, excess paralog-matching variants, and distinct mutational spectra consistent with ongoing gene conversion. Our analysis identifies over 300 individual gene conversion events (GCEs) distributed throughout the Mtb phylogeny. These GCEs occur predominantly within gene families associated with virulence and host–pathogen interactions, including the PE, PPE, and ESX families. Several of the most pronounced diversity hotspots occur in antigens encoded within PRs. Among these, the vaccine candidate PPE18 harbors mutations in validated epitope sequences and predicted alterations in HLA-II binding. Together, these findings demonstrate that gene conversion actively shapes antigenic and virulence-associated diversity in Mtb .

articles_hidden.title: Comparative analysis of photocatalytic, enzymatic, and chemical approaches to identify canonical and noncanonical surfaceomes
articles_hidden.authors: William W. Ho, Yifei Chen, Tomasz Slezak, Oleksandr Zginnyk, Trenton M. Peters-Clarke, Kaitlin Schaefer, Anthony A. Kossiakoff, Kevin K. Leung, James A. Wells
articles_hidden.abstract: The cell surface is a critical nexus in cellular communication and a rich landscape yielding the majority of current therapeutic targets, yet only a small fraction of cell surface proteins have been targeted therapeutically. The cell surface proteome (surfaceome) comprises only ~1% of the human proteome by mass, motivating enrichment strategies to detect surfaceome alterations in disease for drug target discovery. Developments in photocatalytic technology have revolutionized the study of protein neighborhoods around specific targets of interest, but photocatalysis has been underutilized for global surfaceome analysis. Here, we describe five distinct photocatalytic surfaceomics strategies, all without the need for cellular engineering, that apply the photocatalyst Eosin Y attached to different cell surface structures: direct glycan ligation, glycan attachment via two different lectins, membrane insertion, and free in extracellular space. We systematically compare these photocatalytic surfaceomics methods to each other as well as to three established chemical and enzymatic surfaceomics methods. We demonstrate that the different photocatalytic surfaceomics techniques achieve broadly similar canonical cell surface protein enrichment but show some important differences reflective of cell surface attachment mechanism. These mechanistically orthogonal surfaceomics techniques consistently identified numerous nonglycosylated proteins with high concordance, many of which represent an underappreciated class of noncanonical cell surface proteins lacking traditional cell surface protein features that may represent potential drug targets. This study substantially expands options for surfaceomics methods using photocatalytic proximity labeling.

articles_hidden.title: Deconfined criticality between an antiferromagnetic insulator and a nodal d -wave superconductor: A quantum Monte Carlo study
articles_hidden.authors: Chuang Chen, Subir Sachdev, Zi Yang Meng
articles_hidden.abstract: We present a quantum Monte Carlo study of the transition between the insulating Néel state and the nodal d -wave superconductor on the square lattice at half-filling. We access a regime of frustrated magnetic order without a sign problem using a parton representation of the electron in terms of fermionic spinons and bosonic chargons. Both partons move in a background π -flux (so the electron experiences no net flux) and are coupled to a quantum fluctuating SU(2) lattice gauge field. In contrast to earlier studies directly on the electronic degrees of freedom, we find evidence for a second-order deconfined quantum phase transition at which both the Néel and d -wave superconductivity orders vanish continuously. We compute correlators of the spinon-chargon composite with the same quantum numbers as the electron: we find a gapless Dirac dispersion inside the d -wave superconductor, turning into a gapped dispersion in the antiferromagnet.

articles_hidden.title: Mediator-associated proteins and the small RNA–guided Polycomb repressive complex enhance cryptic transcription for transposon exclusion
articles_hidden.authors: Zhihao Zhai, Haoyu He, Tomoko Noto, Mingmei Liucong, Jialuo Li, Julie Saksouk, Yike Liu, Xue Wang, Yujie Liu, Kazufumi Mochizuki, Miao Tian
articles_hidden.abstract: Suppression of transposable elements (TEs) is critical for maintaining genome integrity. The evolutionary arms race between TEs and their eukaryotic host organisms has driven the development of small RNA–dependent mechanisms that specifically suppress TEs while leaving non-TE regions unperturbed. In the binucleated ciliate Tetrahymena , small RNAs (sRNAs) are generated from both TE and non-TE regions of the germline genome, whereas noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) from the TE-free somatic genome target and eliminate non-TE sRNAs, thereby selectively preserving TE-specific sRNAs for guiding TE recognition. Since sRNAs are produced from both strands, the counteracting ncRNAs must also occur bidirectionally. However, the mechanism by which the somatic genome generates ncRNAs from both strands remains unresolved. Here, we show that these ncRNAs arise from widespread cryptic transcription initiated outside canonical promoters and dependent on the developmentally specific Mediator complex–associated proteins Dima1 and Emit2. We further demonstrate that sRNA-guided recruitment of the Tetrahymena Polycomb repressive complex 2 and Dima1 occupancy are mutually reinforcing, promoting local accumulation of RNA polymerase II, which may facilitate cryptic transcription from these loci in a histone methyltransferase-independent manner. Disruption of Dima1 abolishes cryptic transcription, leads to aberrant accumulation of non-TE sRNAs, and results in erroneous genome elimination and cell death. These findings reveal a regulatory circuit involving sRNAs, Polycomb, and the Mediator-associated protein Dima1 that promotes cryptic transcription, thereby ensuring accurate TE exclusion and genome integrity.

articles_hidden.title: Susumu Tonegawa (1939–2026): A molecular biologist who transformed immunology and neuroscience
articles_hidden.authors: Juan J. Lafaille, Thomas J. McHugh
articles_hidden.abstract: Susumu Tonegawa transformed two fields of biology. His discovery of the genetic mechanism generating antibody diversity established the foundations of modern immunology and earned him the 1987 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Remarkably, he then began a second scientific career in neuroscience, pioneering genetic approaches to dissect the molecular and circuit mechanisms of learning and memory and, ultimately, the neuronal ensembles that store specific memories. He was also an ambitious institution builder whose leadership shaped neuroscience at Massachusetts Institute of Technology and RIKEN. As former trainees from his immunology and neuroscience labs, we remember a scientist of extraordinary curiosity, intensity, and intellectual courage, who was never afraid to leave familiar territory in pursuit of a fundamental question.

articles_hidden.title: Random, fragile, or correlated: Mechanisms of synteny decay in mammals
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander S. Moffett, Michele Di Pierro
articles_hidden.abstract: We formalize three models of genome evolution, yielding analytical distributions of synteny block sizes between pairs of genomes. To evaluate each model, we fit theoretical synteny block size distributions to empirical distributions from a comparative analysis of nearly 200 mammalian genomes. Between the random breakage model (RBM), with uniformly distributed breakpoints, the fragile breakage model (FBM) with breakpoint hotspots, and what we term the correlated breakage model (CBM) with pairs of nearby breakpoints, we find that the FBM and CBM are far more consistent with mammalian genome evolution than the RBM. Inferred parameters of each model qualitatively agree with previously calculated rates of mammalian genome evolution. The FBM and CBM perform comparably with each other, suggesting that either model could serve as an improved null model of genome evolution to use in statistical tests for syntenic regions that are unlikely to exist due to random chance.

articles_hidden.title: C1ql2 gates stress vulnerability by regulating microglia-mediated synaptic pruning in the BLA-vHPC circuit
articles_hidden.authors: Chun-Yan Wang, Wei-Zhu Liu, Shuang-Mei Liao, Jing Niu, Han-Qing Pan, Wen-Jie You, Ke Zhao, Bao Ma, Ming-Fen Lu, Jia-Xin Zou, Ping Hu, Wen-Hua Zhang, Bing-Xing Pan
articles_hidden.abstract: Synaptic remodeling in emotional circuits contributes to the development of stress-related emotional disorders. However, such remodeling generally exhibits considerable heterogeneity across specific neuronal populations and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identified C1ql2 as a key molecular regulator that governs projection-specific synaptic vulnerability within basolateral amygdala (BLA). Transcriptional profiling revealed that C1ql2 expression is enriched in BLA neurons projecting to ventral hippocampus (BLA →vHPC PNs), but not in those projecting to nucleus accumbens (NAc), and is significantly down-regulated following chronic social defeat stress (CSDS). Gain- and loss-of-function manipulations demonstrated that C1ql2 regulates stress-induced neuronal remodeling in BLA →vHPC PNs, including dendritic hypertrophy, synaptic outgrowth, and enhanced glutamatergic transmission, thereby shaping susceptibility to anxiety-like behavior. We further found that CSDS-induced C1ql2 loss impairs microglial engulfment of BLA →vHPC PNs synapses, leading to aberrant synaptic accumulation. Our findings establish C1ql2-mediated neuron-microglia cross talk that critically regulates circuit-specific synaptic pathophysiology in stress-related disorders.

articles_hidden.title: The revised diploid genome sequence of an individual human: A workflow for near telomere-to-telomere assemblies using only Oxford Nanopore Technologies Simplex-reads
articles_hidden.authors: Si Lok, Timothy N. H. Lau, Amy H. Y. Tong, Brett Trost, Miriam S. Reuter, Bhooma Thiruvahindrapuram, Tara A. Paton, Jeffrey R. MacDonald, Lynette Y. S. Lau, Christian R. Marshall, J. Craig Venter, Stephen W. Scherer
articles_hidden.abstract: The first draft diploid genome assembly (HuRef) of an individual in 2007 was a milestone in genomics. Here, we report HuRef2.0, a revision of HuRef assembled using only Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) Simplex-reads and the hifiasm assembler. Results are close in continuity to the telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assemblies but were assembled from standard DNA samples without using multiple sequencing and mapping technologies, including ultra-long-reads and/or proximity-ligation. Three ONT flowcells (~103× coverage) from fresh blood DNA produced an assembly comprising 26 contigs, with gapless assembly of 23 chromosomes (Chr). Two gaps on ChrY were locally assembled to yield the final T2T-assembly, HuRef2.0, with base accuracy >Q60.34 and 2,393 phase blocks with an NG50 value of 2.36 Mb. Assembly from a single ONT flowcell (~35× coverage) consistently produced an assembly more contiguous than GRCh38.p14, providing a foundation for further optimization and scaling. Assembly quality was assessed by direct chromosome-level alignments to a reference genome, variant calling, and annotation of gene-rich regions at Chr22q11, the extended MHC locus, and at several difficult to assemble regions, including the rRNA gene clusters, the subtelomeric region on Chr4q35, ChrY, and the centromeres. More accurate but shorter Pacific Biosciences HiFi-reads produced less contiguous assemblies than from equivalent coverage of error-corrected ONT reads, indicating the importance of read-length. We compared HuRef2.0 to an assembly of a low-passage EBV-transformed lymphoblastoid cell line derived from the same donor. At least at a 400 kb resolution, we did not observe notable structural differences in the two assemblies.

articles_hidden.title: Contactless continuous guidance of matter in its main states using curved elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields
articles_hidden.authors: Dmitrii Nikolaev, Denys Iablonskyi, Alexander Martinez-Marchese, Marika Sirkka, Mikel Aldea, Chinedum Okwudire, Edward Hæggström, Asier Marzo, Ari Salmi
articles_hidden.abstract: Acoustic manipulation uses sound waves to exert force on matter, enabling contactless movement, trapping, and the structuring of particles in bulk media. It offers a contamination-free approach for handling matter in applications spanning across chemistry, biology, and advanced manufacturing. However, state-of-the-art techniques, including acoustic holograms or phased arrays of transducers (PATs) are limited to transporting individual particles or small clusters one by one, and are not suitable for dispersed matter such as gases or aerosols. Here, we introduce a method for guiding a continuous flow of matter along reconfigurable three-dimensional trajectories using elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields (EBAFs). These fields generate converging radial acoustic forces along a programmable path, forming stable mid-air conduits that continuously transport matter. Compared to existing methods such as near-field acoustic levitation, acoustofluidic separation, particle manipulation with vortex and Airy beams, the proposed method offers enhanced versatility, scalability, and real-time control of transport trajectories in mid-air without requiring physical guiding structures. We developed methods to generate EBAFs with PATs tailored to different particle sizes and material properties, and experimentally demonstrated guidance of solids, liquids, aerosols, and gases along programmable trajectories. This technique enables containerless laboratory operations, precise and contamination-free reagent or energy delivery, and integration into advanced additive manufacturing processes that require controlled distribution of matter in different states to target zones.

articles_hidden.title: Lhx9 specifically modulates phalanx number, whereas Lhx2 constrains digit length in tetrapods
articles_hidden.authors: Yining Tang, Shibin Bai, Shanshan Li, Ying Mao, Wanyi Dang, Huiling Xue, Songyang Shang, Ziqiu Jia, Xiaoping Li, Yanlei Liu, Xiaona Xu, David M. Irwin, Junpeng Zhang, Shuyi Zhang, Zhe Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Most nonmammalian tetrapods exhibit more than three phalanges in their posterior digits (III–V), whereas mammals are restricted to no more than three. So far, the molecular mechanism underlying this evolutionary reduction and the functions of Lhx2 and Lhx9 in digit development remain unclear. Here we show divergent evolution of Lhx2 and Lhx9 expression patterns in embryonic limbs across tetrapods. We further demonstrate that although ectopic overexpression of each gene in chick embryos delayed limb skeletal development, only Lhx9 reduced the phalanx number in the posterior digits. Transcriptomic analysis showed that Lhx2 regulates pathways for chondrocyte and osteoblast differentiation, and Lhx9 preferentially influences skeletal segmentation via the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) pathway. The unique function and differential expression of Lhx9 in the limb buds between mammals and nonmammalian tetrapods suggest it may have acquired a role in suppressing phalanx number, driving the evolutionary reduction of phalanx number in mammals.

articles_hidden.title: Geography of groundwater use and depletion in internationally shared aquifers
articles_hidden.authors: Marc F. Müller, Kyle F. Davis, Julie Faure, Davide Danilo Chiarelli, Fengwei Hung
articles_hidden.abstract: Transboundary aquifers (TBAs) underlie 35% of global groundwater-irrigated cropland, yet few are covered by formal cooperative arrangements. Whether this limited cooperation is consequential depends in part on where groundwater is used within shared aquifers, because pumping far from international borders may generate little cross-border impact. Combining ∼ 116,000 well observations with global irrigation data across all 426 known TBAs, we assess how groundwater use and depletion differ from comparable domestic systems and how they are distributed relative to international borders. While we find no evidence of greater average depletion in TBAs, depletion is more strongly concentrated toward international borders in shared aquifers and varies substantially across systems. Irrigation is also more intensive and concentrated toward borders in shared aquifers, although much of this pattern is attenuated after accounting for border rivers. Groundwater-supplied irrigation remains more border-proximate after accounting for these rivers. A dyad-level typology distinguishes shared systems according to where groundwater demand is concentrated, linking their potential for cross-border interaction to different management options. These findings suggest that transboundary groundwater governance should be organized around the geography of groundwater use and potential cross-border interactions rather than treating shared aquifers as uniform governance units.

articles_hidden.title: Connexins are essential for the contribution of latent progenitors to healing after spinal cord injury
articles_hidden.authors: María Victoria Falco, Gabriela Fabbiani, Daniel Prieto, Mateo Vidal, Milagros Benítez, María Inés Rehermann, María Constanza Silvera, Renata Simeone, Federico F. Trigo, Raúl E. Russo
articles_hidden.abstract: Gap junctions are important regulators of the biology of neural stem cells. Both in vertebrates with regenerative abilities and neonatal rodents, ependymal cells communicate via connexin (Cx) 43 and Cx26. Gap junction coupling and Cx26 are down-regulated as the ependyma becomes quiescent in adulthood, but injury overrules this developmental down-regulation suggesting a role for Cx signaling in the reactivation of ependymal cells. However, direct evidence of the involvement of these Cxs in the reactivation of the ependymal stem cell niche is lacking. Here, we aim to explore the role of Cx26 and Cx43 in the response of ependymal cells to injury by means of specific genetic deletion. We find that Cx26 is critical for the proliferative response of ependymal cells to injury. The reduced response of ependymal cells by Cx26 deletion increased the extension of the lesion because of impaired healing resulting from a weak contribution of the ependymal stem cell niche. On the other hand, Cx43—via gap junction coupling and hemichannels—plays a key role in the communication of Ca 2+ signals between ependymal cells induced by activation of P2X7 receptors. Our data show that Cxs are relevant targets to manipulate the ependymal stem cell niche to achieve better healing after spinal cord injury.

articles_hidden.title: Mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation driven by energetic-particle irradiation of icy solids
articles_hidden.authors: Gerardo Dominguez, Caroline Caplan, Lauren Tafla, Joshua Lucas, Ming-Chang Liu, Kevin McKeegan, Jeff Gillis
articles_hidden.abstract: Mass-independent isotope fractionation (MIF) of oxygen provides key insights into atmospheric chemistry and the origin of isotopic anomalies in planetary materials. To date, MIF has been primarily associated with gas-phase processes involving symmetry-dependent reaction pathways, most notably ozone formation. Whether analogous effects can arise in condensed phases or at interfaces remains an open question. Here we report laboratory experiments demonstrating that energetic particle irradiation of icy oxide surfaces produces mass-independent oxygen isotope fractionation at temperatures as low as 10 K. Electron irradiation of SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 substrates in the presence of H 2 O ice results in measurable shifts in Δ 17 O in the underlying solids. The resulting three-isotope relationships include slope-1-like behavior in SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 and distinct, substrate-dependent trends in Al 2 O 3 , indicating that irradiation-induced defect formation and interfacial chemistry govern the isotope effects. The magnitude of the observed anomalies demonstrates that irradiation-driven processes can generate substantial oxygen isotope heterogeneity in condensed phases. These results identify a previously unrecognized class of MIF and provide a quantitative framework for interpreting oxygen isotope signatures in radiation-processed environments, including interstellar grains and early solar system materials.

articles_hidden.title: Local growth laws determine global shape of molluscan shells
articles_hidden.authors: Huan Liu, Kaushik Bhattacharya
articles_hidden.abstract: Molluscan shells come in various shapes and sizes. Despite this diversity, each species produces a shell with a characteristic shape that is independent of environmental conditions. We seek to understand this robust complexity. We are guided by two principles in the spirit of D’Arcy Thompson. First, the growth is governed by the repeated and continuous application of a fixed growth law, even as the shell evolves in overall shape, without any complex biological machinery to monitor and control the growth. Second, the growth law depends solely on local geometry at the shell’s growing edge. The first principle naturally leads to the mathematical statement that the shape of the shell is generated by the action of a Lie group on a protoconch. The second naturally leads to a particular representation of the Lie group. We use this representation to show that the shapes of nearly all known molluscan shells can be described by essentially three parameters: a scalar (scaling), a vector (orientation), and a curve (edge of the protoconch). We relate these parameters to the phylogenetic tree. In addition to the morphogenetic insight, our results potentially point to a alternative growth-based approach to engineering complex structures.

articles_hidden.title: Immense but not immutable: A sudden and sustained decline in deep-pelagic life in a large oceanic ecosystem
articles_hidden.authors: Tracey T. Sutton, Rosanna J. Milligan, April B. Cook, Kevin M. Boswell, Heather Bracken-Grissom, Tamara Frank, Heather Judkins, Jon A. Moore, Isabel C. Romero, Michael Vecchione, Marta D’Elia, Matthew W. Johnston, Pedro A. Peres, Nina M. Pruzinsky, John A. Quinlan, Joseph D. Warren, Daniel R. Hahn
articles_hidden.abstract: The deep-pelagic habitat of the Gulf of Mexico comprises 90.4% of its volume and houses an exceptionally diverse deep-pelagic animal community that provides numerous ecosystem services, including carbon cycling and prey provisioning for oceanic predators. Here, we report sudden, severe, and persistent declines in the abundance of deep-pelagic fishes, crustaceans, and cephalopods that have persisted for over a decade. Over a 3.5-y period, animal abundances declined by 60 to 85%, taxon depending. Particularly hard-hit were ecologically foundational taxa such as euphausiids and lanternfishes. The magnitude of population-level decline that occurred during this 3.5-y period was greater than any observed over a 60-y period in the California Current system, the only comparable dataset, making this the fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type. These declines were detected both via direct sampling and acoustic sensing, providing independent corroboration. Genomic analyses indicate reductions in genetic diversity among dominant taxa, both a corroboration and a consequence of the decline. Furthermore, resource managers report that these trends parallel those of managed or protected Gulf species that are dependent on deep-pelagic prey, including endangered species (e.g., beaked whales, Rice’s whale). No naturally occurring factors (e.g., temperature, oxygen, food supply) correlated with the observed declines, suggesting an anthropogenic proximate cause. That the declines began shortly after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill points to that event as the most parsimonious explanation. These findings suggest that despite its immense size the deep-pelagic biome is vulnerable to human-induced disturbance and possesses limited resilience to facilitate recovery.

articles_hidden.title: Modeling the global potential of smart farming innovations
articles_hidden.authors: Shahrear Roman, Hadi Hadi, Wyclife Agumba Oluoch, David Zilberman, Robert Finger, David Wuepper
articles_hidden.abstract: Smart farming innovations can improve agricultural productivity, resilience, and environmental sustainability, yet their real-world impact hinges on their diffusion dynamics, which in turn depend on their economic viability. We present here a global assessment of the profitability of smart farming innovation across croplands at a spatial resolution of ~5 km from the farmers’ and the societal perspectives. We cover application mapping for precision agriculture, automated application of inputs, autonomous weeding machines, GPS steering assistance systems, and autonomous irrigation systems. For this, we compiled a globally comprehensive dataset of smart farming innovation adoption locations (N = 4,422) based on a combination of a survey (N = 2,677) and a meta-analysis (N = 1,745) and combined them with remotely sensed and statistical data to train an ensemble of five geospatial machine learning models (generalized linear models, random forests, support vector machines, maximum entropy, and boosted regression trees), which show the global distribution of the different innovations’ profitability and its overlap with major environmental issues the innovations can help to mitigate. Simulations of future socioeconomic pathways combined with assumptions about future agri-environmental policies reveal that, especially in middle-income countries, the potential of smart farming will grow over time.

articles_hidden.title: Superlubricity by glycerosome boundary layers
articles_hidden.authors: Yihui Dong, Wei Cao, Roman Kamyshinsky, Nir Kampf, Panpan Zhao, Yaelle Schilt, Uri Raviv, Jacob Klein
articles_hidden.abstract: The search for high-performance lubricants is of broad relevance to biomedical applications, including artificial joints, regenerative scaffolds, and osteoarthritis therapies. Here we introduce glycerosomes—phosphatidylcholine (PC)-based vesicles containing glycerol—as a promising boundary lubricant. Using a surface force balance, we show that glycerosomes achieve a friction coefficient as low as 10 − 5 under a high compression pressure of 15.6 MPa, representing a 20-fold reduction compared to conventional PC liposomes. This level of lubrication surpasses any previously reported boundary lubricant system at such pressures in aqueous media. Mechanistically, glycerosomes exhibit substantially lower adhesion energy than PC liposomes, and theoretical simulations reveal enhanced vesicle stability and flexibility. Our findings establish glycerosomes as a superior hydration lubrication platform, with promising implications for both biomedical implants and industrial applications requiring robust lubricity.

articles_hidden.title: Harry L. Swinney: Nonlinear science and chaos pioneer
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Lathrop, Michael Schatz, Katepalli Sreenivasan
articles_hidden.abstract: Harry Leonard Swinney passed away peacefully at his home in Austin, Texas, on July 13, 2026, at the age of 87. Harry was an exceptional experimental physicist, well-known for elegant studies of instabilities, nonlinear dynamics, chaos and pattern formation in a wide variety of fluid, chemical, and granular systems, work whose influence propagated into numerous scientific and engineering disciplines well beyond the particular problems that prompted it. The late Russell Donnelly of the University of Oregon used to say, “Harry is a prince”; Russ meant it, in the spirit of the tenth-century Persian poet Ferdowsi, as a compliment affirming the nobility, dignity, integrity, and grace with which Harry pursued his science and treated everyone he worked alongside.
